title: Filesystem is full
summary: Writes fail with no space left. Find what is consuming it before deleting anything.

steps.title: See which filesystem is actually full
steps.look: The Use% column, and note the mount point. A full /var is a very different problem from a full /home.

signals.means: Container or snap storage, not the host's own data.

steps.title: Check inodes, because df can lie
steps.look: Space free but IUse% at 100 means inode exhaustion. The error is identical but the fix is completely different.

steps.title: Find the largest directories
steps.look: The -x keeps it on one filesystem so you are not misled by other mounts. Work downward from the largest entry.

steps.title: Find space held by deleted but still-open files
steps.look: A deleted file held open by a running process still occupies disk. This explains the case where du shows far less than df.

signals.means: Space is held by a deleted file still open. Restarting that process releases it.

causes.cause: Log files grew without rotation.
causes.fix: Truncate with : > file rather than deleting, so the open handle stays valid. Then fix logrotate.

causes.cause: A process holds a deleted file open.
causes.fix: Restart that process. No amount of deleting will reclaim the space otherwise.

causes.cause: Inodes exhausted by many small files.
causes.fix: Find the directory with the most entries and clear it. Often a session or cache directory.

causes.cause: Container images and layers.
causes.fix: Prune the container runtime's storage, with a time filter rather than wholesale.

verify: The write that was failing now succeeds.
Rotation or cleanup is configured so it does not recur.
escalate: Whether any deleted files are still held open

title: Address already in use
summary: A service will not start because something already holds its port.

steps.title: Find what is listening
steps.look: The process name and PID in the last column. Without sudo you will not see the owner for another user's process.

signals.means: A process holds it. The name and PID are in the parentheses.
Nothing is listening, so the failure is something else.

steps.title: Check whether it is bound on a different interface
steps.look: 0.0.0.0 versus 127.0.0.1 versus a specific IP. Two processes can bind the same port on different addresses, which looks contradictory until you see this.

steps.title: Check for a socket stuck in TIME_WAIT
steps.look: TIME_WAIT entries without a listener mean the old socket has not been released. SO_REUSEADDR in the application is the correct fix, not waiting.

steps.title: Stop the process holding the port
steps.look: Re-run ss to confirm the port is free before starting your service.
steps.note: Terminates the process. If it is a production service, its clients drop immediately. Confirm what the PID actually is with ps before running this, and prefer the service manager's stop command so it shuts down cleanly.

causes.cause: Another process is bound to the port.
causes.fix: Stop it through its service manager, or configure your service to use a different port.

causes.cause: An old socket has not been released.
causes.fix: Enable SO_REUSEADDR in the application. Waiting works but is not a fix.

causes.cause: Bound to a specific address that overlaps your wildcard bind.
causes.fix: Bind to a specific address instead of 0.0.0.0.

causes.cause: A systemd socket unit holds the port.
causes.fix: Stop the .socket unit, not just the .service.

verify: The service starts and is listening.
ss shows it as the owner of the port.
escalate: Whether it is managed by systemd

title: systemd service will not start
summary: systemctl start fails or the unit restarts in a loop. The journal has the real reason.

steps.title: Read the unit's current state and last lines
steps.look: The Active line and the exit status. 'code=exited status=N' is the application's own exit code and the most useful number on the screen.

signals.means: systemd could not execute the binary. Wrong path, or not executable.
The configured User does not exist.
It started but never signalled readiness in time.

steps.title: Read the journal for this unit's last start
steps.look: The application's own output. systemctl status truncates; this does not.

steps.title: Validate the unit file itself
steps.look: Syntax problems and unresolvable references that status will never mention.

steps.title: Reload systemd after editing a unit
steps.look: No output means success. Start the unit again afterwards.
steps.note: Re-reads all unit files. Running services are not restarted and nothing is interrupted, but forgetting this after an edit means systemd keeps using the old definition and your change appears to do nothing.

causes.cause: ExecStart points at something that cannot be executed.
causes.fix: Use an absolute path and check the execute bit. systemd does not use your shell's PATH.

causes.cause: The User directive names an account that does not exist.
causes.fix: Create the user or correct the name.

causes.cause: WorkingDirectory does not exist.
causes.fix: Create it, or remove the directive.

causes.cause: Type=notify or forking, but the process does not behave that way.
causes.fix: Use Type=simple for a process that stays in the foreground. This mismatch causes start timeouts constantly.

causes.cause: The unit file was edited without a daemon-reload.
causes.fix: Run systemctl daemon-reload after every unit file change.

verify: systemctl status shows active and running.
It survives a reboot if it is enabled.
The journal shows a clean startup.
escalate: journalctl for the last start attempt

title: Load average is high and the box feels slow
summary: High load can mean CPU, disk wait or thread explosion. They look identical at first and need different fixes.

steps.title: Separate CPU from I/O wait
steps.look: The %Cpu line. High us means real computation; high wa means processes blocked on disk; high sy means kernel overhead, often context switching.

signals.means: Significant I/O wait. The disk, not the CPU, is the bottleneck.
Steal time. The hypervisor is taking cycles; this is a noisy-neighbour problem.

steps.title: Compare load against core count
steps.look: Load equal to core count is fully busy, not broken. Load at several times the core count is where queuing hurts.

steps.title: Find the top consumers
steps.look: The elapsed time column matters as much as the CPU column. A process at 100% for three seconds is normal; for three hours it is not.

steps.title: Check whether processes are blocked rather than running
steps.look: State D is uninterruptible sleep, almost always disk or NFS. Load counts these, which is why a box can show high load with idle CPUs.

causes.cause: Processes are blocked on disk.
causes.fix: Find the process doing the I/O. The CPU is not the constraint and adding cores will not help.

causes.cause: One process is consuming the CPU.
causes.fix: Identify it from the elapsed time. Restart or throttle it depending on what it is.

causes.cause: A large number of threads or processes.
causes.fix: Check the thread count. An unbounded worker pool is a common cause.

causes.cause: The hypervisor is taking CPU time.
causes.fix: This is not fixable from inside the guest. Raise it with the platform owner.

causes.cause: Load is roughly equal to core count under real work.
causes.fix: Nothing is wrong. Measure response time rather than load average.

verify: Load is proportional to core count under normal work.
The specific contributor was identified, not just observed.
escalate: Top processes by CPU with elapsed time

title: SSH permission denied (publickey)
summary: The server rejected your key. Verbose output names the exact reason.

steps.title: Run with verbose output and read which keys were offered
steps.look: Which keys the client offered and which methods the server accepts. If your key was never offered, the problem is local, not on the server.

signals.means: The key was offered and rejected. The problem is server-side authorization.
The key file does not exist at the path the client expects.
The private key is readable by others, so ssh refuses to use it.

steps.title: Check local key permissions
steps.look: The private key must be 600 and the directory 700. ssh silently refuses keys that are more permissive.

steps.title: Confirm which key the client will use for this host
steps.look: The resolved config. A ~/.ssh/config entry may be pointing at a different key than you assume.

steps.title: Check the server side if you have another way in
steps.look: sshd states the precise reason, including permission problems on the remote authorized_keys file, which the client can never see.

causes.cause: The public key is not in the remote authorized_keys.
causes.fix: Add it. Confirm you copied the .pub file, not the private key.

causes.cause: Local private key permissions are too open.
causes.fix: chmod 600 on the key and 700 on ~/.ssh.

causes.cause: The remote ~/.ssh or authorized_keys is group-writable.
causes.fix: chmod 700 ~/.ssh and 600 authorized_keys on the server. sshd refuses them otherwise and logs the reason.

causes.cause: The key file is not where the client looks.
causes.fix: Point at it with -i, or add an IdentityFile entry to ~/.ssh/config.

causes.cause: Correct key, wrong username.
causes.fix: Cloud images each have their own default user. ubuntu, ec2-user and admin are not interchangeable.

verify: SSH connects without a password prompt.
It works from a fresh shell, not only with an explicit -i flag.
escalate: ssh -vvv output around the authentication attempt
auth.log from the server if reachable

title: Process was killed by the OOM killer
summary: A process vanished with no error. The kernel killed it to reclaim memory.

steps.title: Confirm the kernel did it
steps.look: The timestamp, the process name and its RSS at the moment of death. This is definitive; without it you are only guessing.

signals.means: Confirmed. The kernel chose this process as the victim.
A cgroup limit, not the whole host. Only that container or unit was constrained.

steps.title: See the current memory picture
steps.look: available, not free. Linux uses free memory for cache by design, so a low free number is normal and not a problem.

steps.title: Find the current biggest consumers
steps.look: RSS in kilobytes. Compare the top entry against total memory to see whether one process dominates.

steps.title: Check what the kernel would kill next
steps.cmd: for p in $(pgrep {process}); do echo "$p $(cat /proc/$p/oom_score)"; done
steps.look: Higher score means more likely to be chosen. Useful for predicting the next victim before it happens.

causes.cause: The host ran out of memory.
causes.fix: Reduce the workload, add memory, or set limits so one process cannot take everything.

causes.cause: A container or systemd unit hit its own limit.
causes.fix: Raise MemoryMax or the container limit, having measured the real requirement first.

causes.cause: No swap, so there is no buffer before the killer runs.
causes.fix: A small swap file gives the kernel room to reclaim before killing. Not a substitute for enough RAM.

causes.cause: Memory grows without bound.
causes.fix: Profile the process. The OOM killer is a symptom, not the problem.

verify: The process stays running through a full workload cycle.
A limit exists so one process cannot take the whole host.
